Summary
In this chapter, you learned about object orientation, a concept that is exhibited
throughout the rest of the book. Because of its structure of GameObjects with
components, Unity is perfectly designed for an OOP mindset. You also learned about
component-oriented design, a programming design pattern that works very well with
Unity and—while a bit more complicated to implement—can make your code simpler
and more manageable.
Along with the idea of component-oriented OOP comes the concept of modularity. In
many ways, modular code is the opposite of monolithic code. Modular coding focuses
on making small, reusable functions and classes that do one thing really well. Because
modular classes and functions are small (usually fewer than 500 lines), they are easier to
debug and understand. Modular code is also designed to be reusable.
In the following chapter, you'll learn about data-oriented design and Unity's new Data-
Oriented Tech Stack (DOTS). DOTS encompasses several new technologies that Unity is
moving toward, which have the potential to drastically increase the performance of our
Unity games but require a very different mindset than OOP (and as of Unity 2020.3 are
not yet fully implemented).
After that, you'll start Part III of the book, a series of focused tutorials that will help you
learn how to start prototypes for various kinds of games. I hope you enjoy what you find
there and can use them to start your journey as a designer, prototyper, and developer.

DATA-ORIENTED DESIGN
While object-oriented programming has been
the dominant form of programming taught
over the past four decades, it may surprise you
to learn that object-oriented code doesn't work
at all well with modern memory architecture
or multi-threaded computer processors. The
alternative is data-oriented design. While not
necessary in most projects, when needed,
Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack can cause
code execution speed to increase by up to one
thousand times!
In this chapter you will learn about DOTS
and get a glimpse of the possible future
of programming, along with a DOTS code
tutorial.

The Theory of Data-Oriented Design
Data-Oriented Design (DOD) is not new, but it has seen a resurgence over the last two
decades, driven especially by the limitations of console hardware and the ways in which
processors and graphics cards have improved recently. The core concept of DOD is that
all programming is data manipulation,
1
and efficient programming is code that considers
how that data is actually used and transferred by the processor.
Realities of Modern Computer Hardware
There are several technological considerations that are addressed by Data-Oriented
Design:
2
The Limitations of Moore's Law
In 1965, Gordon Moore, the co-founder of Fairchild Semiconductor and eventual CEO
of Intel, predicted a yearly doubling of transistors in integrated circuits for at least a
decade. In 1975, he revised this to a doubling every two years. This prediction held true
so consistently that it became known as "Moore's Law." Every two years or so, the perfor-
mance of a central processing unit (CPU), the main processor of a computer, doubled as
individual transistors got smaller and smaller—until it became extremely difficult to make
them any smaller (to the point that individual wires on chips are only a couple atoms
thick!). Starting in 2010, this had a profound effect on processor speed and design.
As you can see in the chart in Figure 28.1 by Karl Rupp, though the number of transis-
tors continues to increase, single-thread performance and clock speed (i.e., frequency
[MHz]) have stopped increasing. However, the number of logical cores started increas-
ing exponentially in about 2005, which brings us to…
Increasing Numbers of Processor Cores
Now, nearly all processors in computers, game consoles, and mobile devices are multi-
core, meaning that rather than a single ridiculously large processor, they instead have
a CPU containing several smaller processors that work in parallel. However, computer
code for parallel processing is notoriously difficult to write. So even now, even though
my computer's processor has eight cores, most code in Unity still executes in a single

Data Locality and Access Speed
While your processor—any processor you own—is objectively very fast, it doesn't mat-
ter how fast it is if it doesn't have the data it needs at hand. All processors can only act

time it will take for the computer to access it. A computer has several different levels of
data access, and each subsequent level holds more data but takes significantly longer
to access. In 2010, Dr. Jeff Dean (current lead of Google AI) gave a somewhat famous
talk

previous decade at Google. The salient one for us here is his "Numbers Everyone Should
Know," which described access times at various levels of the computer. You can see an
updated (and simplified) version of this in Figure 28.2.

Cache Lines
The last core computer engineering concept that you need to understand is cache lines.
When your processor moves data from RAM into one of its caches (or from one cache to

a time, which is referred to as a cache line (equivalent to sixteen 32-bit integers (or floats),
eight 4-byte RGBA colors, or about five 3-float positions). Because of cache lines, if all the
data you need is located close to each other in RAM, you get something called a cache
hit, when the processor can act on the next piece of data without having to resort to
pulling the data from RAM. Additionally, modern processors will attempt to predict what
RAM data they will need next and prefetch that data from RAM into a cache. So if large
amounts of data are organized well, the computer can correctly predict what it needs to
pull into caches and greatly increase performance. If your data is organized well, that is
good data locality. On the other hand, bad data locality leads to frequent cache misses.

your computer, tablet, or mobile phone work, we can take a look at what's wrong with

and the programmer's lack of ability to manage data locality in OOP.

To move a GameObject, you really only need to know two things about it: its position

Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack
Data-oriented design focuses first and foremost on data locality: getting the right data in
the right place for the processor to handle it efficiently. By organizing data efficiently and
managing access to that data, Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack (DOTS
8
) solves most
of the data issues present in Unity's traditional OOP approach. Unity DOTS comprises
three core technologies that collaborate to provide what Unity calls "performance by
default"; that is, code that is performant due to its structure without requiring addi-
tional optimization. The three technologies are:
9
■ C# Job System: A highly optimized code library that allows developers to write safe
multithreaded code.
■ Burst Compiler: By limiting certain "high level" aspects of the C# language, Unity
is able to compile C# code into assembly language that runs faster than C++ code on
the same processor.
■ Entity Component System (ECS): A new paradigm for code organization based
entirely on data-oriented design. Unity ECS also includes the tools to convert Unity
GameObjects to this new paradigm.
Unfortunately, at this time, Unity ECS is still incomplete. Throughout most of the months
that I was writing the third edition of this book, Unity ECS changed so frequently that

Now that's more like it! On my laptop, just enabling Burst Compile on the PerlinIPage

a single line of code, and it shows the power of the Burst Compiler. This is also more

kind of magic. The short version is that regular C# has some specific features that make
it easy to write code but very difficult to compile that code efficiently. The Burst Com-
piler prevents us from using those specific features, which allows it to compile extremely
efficient code. Through testing, Unity has found that machine language compiled by
the Burst Compiler is faster and more efficient than comparable machine language
compiled from C++.

Through use of the C# Job System and Burst Compiler, we were able to create a more
complex version of our procedural image generation that ran at considerably higher
speeds, but there's one major pillar of Unity DOTS that we haven't talked about yet.
Entity Component Systems (ECS)
I didn't cover ECS in the tutorial because as I write this book, Unity's version is still in the
Preview state, and it's changing very frequently. I wrote several ECS examples over the
course of authoring this edition, and every one that I made would no longer compile
just a few months after I wrote it because Unity ECS had changed so much. However,
the theory of ECS is stable, and that is what I'll describe here.
Outside of Unity's implementation, ECS comprises three core concepts:
■ Entities: Conceptually, these are similar to GameObjects, but the actual Entity is just
a single unsigned int that groups a collection of Components.

■ Systems: Functions that act on Entities that have the right set of Components. Also

Components Are Molecules of Data
In ECS, the objects in the game are broken down into Components, which I like to think
of as "molecular" chunks of data—they're not the smallest possible bits (i.e., not atomic);
rather, they're the smallest chunk that you would always need to group. For example,
a 2D position will always need float values for x and y, so storing them together as a
float makes sense. So, you could create a &oPBPosition Component as shown in

small. As molecular data, Components are the smallest chunk of data that you would

Systems Act on Groups of Components
In ECS, Systems are not associated with specific Entities or types of Entities at all. Instead
every System is designed to act on any and every Entity that has the Components it's

ECS Storage Minimizes Cache Misses
As shown in Figure 28.18, the Components of all Entities are stored together in arrays of
each Component type. This greatly improves data locality. The example SysB8pdate

An Entity Is an Index
With data organized by Component, the best way to think of an Entity is as an index
that tells you which &oPBPosition, &oPB9elocity, &oPBRotation, and other Compo-
nents in the various arrays all belong together in each Entity.
Because an Entity is a simple index used to find the right Components (as opposed to
a class, which contains memory references to its data), SysB8pdatePosition never
requests any data other than the two Components it needs; none of the other Compo-
nents that are part of each Entity are ever pulled from RAM into cache memory.
The Benefits of ECS
"Performance by default" is Unity's tagline for DOTS, and it is well-earned. The core
structure of ECS ensures that your code is set up very well for data locality, the C# Job
System, and the Burst Compiler, all of which maximize speed and efficiency on mod-
ern processors. Additionally, developers with experience in ECS state that though the
initial transition to ECS was painful, after it was implemented, both the addition of new
features and the debugging of existing features were drastically simpler.

The Future of Unity DOTS
Though Unity has committed to DOTS for a few years now, their attitude about it seems
to have shifted. Initially, the messaging was along the lines of "You'll never use OOP
again!" —which was pretty frightening to a lot of people who had spent years learn-
ing both object-oriented programming and the subtleties of how to code for Unity C#.
Lately, this has transitioned to "You should use DOTS when you need it," and "If you
design for DOTS from the beginning, your project will be more performant and simpler
to maintain."
Unity has also begun replacing some of its core code libraries with DOTS versions,
including a Unity Physics system (developed with Havok to replace the older NVIDIA
PhysX system) and new networking code. The Unity Physics system
31
is already working
quite well and incorporates several very cool enhancements, like allowing you to run
multiple physics simulations simultaneously and allowing you to run predictive physics
(e.g., showing the player where all the balls on a pool table will go). The DOTS-based

NetCode networking library is still quite far from release, though some impressive
demos have been created with it.
As I mentioned earlier in the chapter, Unity's ECS library has changed drastically and
rapidly throughout its development. The largest reason for this seems to be that Unity
is working very hard to make ECS code less daunting. So, rather than expecting devel-
opers to create Entities, Components, and Systems from scratch, Unity has created a
conversion workflow that allows developers to create GameObjects in Unity like normal,
which are then converted automatically into Entities at runtime. Beyond explicit conver-
sions, I expect Unity to continue to transition under-the-hood code to DOTS, granting
all developers some benefits of DOTS while still supporting more traditional Unity
development workflows and coding.
To learn more about Unity's strategy around DOTS, I recommend checking out the
Unity DOTS website at https://unity.com/dots .
Unity also gave an excellent series of DOTS talks at Unite Copenhagen 2019, which you
can find by searching for "Unite Copenhagen 2019 DOTS" on YouTube.com. In particu-
lar, Mike Geig does an excellent job of making the case for DOTS in his talk "Converting
Your Game to DOTS."

Summary
In this chapter, you've glimpsed a bit of the future and gotten a chance to explore a
bit of DOTS code and concepts. There is much more to be learned, and by the time
you read this, DOTS and the resources about it will be better than they are as I write it.
However, if this chapter was daunting to you, it's important to keep in mind that you
can write an excellent game without worrying about DOTS at all, and millions of people
around the world are using Unity to do just that!
The next part of the book will take you through several tutorials to help you learn how
to make various kinds of games and take advantage of various features of Unity. All of
those tutorials are built using object-oriented programming because doing so is still the
best way to learn Unity and start prototyping your game ideas as quickly as possible.
After you've gained more experience with Unity development, I recommend exploring
DOTS further and seeing how it can improve the performance of your games.

What You Will Learn
As the first in our series of tutorials, you'll learn several new concepts and review
some from Part II of the book, including:
■ Moving a GameObject to follow the mouse
■ Using InYoNe() to call a function after a specified delay
■ Time-based movement of GameObjects
■ Randomizing the movement of GameObjects
■ Displaying score and high score on screen
■ Using PlayerPrefs to track high score across multiple games
■ Using Physics Layers to specify which GameObjects will collide with others
■ and much more!
Figure 29.1 The finished Apple Picker prototype
The Apple Picker Prototype
In this chapter, you'll make Apple Picker, which you can see in Figure 29.1. It's the
simple game that we outlined in Chapter 16, "Thinking in Digital Systems." If
you didn't read that chapter, it might be worthwhile to go back and check out
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
the PUrPose oF a dIGItal PrototyPe 623
the chapter's "Game Analysis: Apple Picker " section, where I went over flow-
charts of how each object in the game needs to act.
Apple Picker is based on the classic Atari game Kaboom!. In the game, an AppleTree
moves back and forth dropping Apples that players attempt to catch with three Baskets.
Each Apple that is caught by the player is worth 100 points. If the player misses one
Apple, then all Apples on screen disappear, the player loses one Basket, and the game
continues. When all three Baskets have been lost, the game is over.
The Purpose of a Digital Prototype
Before we start making the prototype of Apple Picker, now's probably a good time to
think again about the purpose of a digital prototype. The first part of the book provided
considerable discussion of paper prototypes and why they are useful. Paper game
prototypes help you do the following:
■ Test, reject, and/or refine game mechanics and rules quickly
■ Explore the dynamic behavior of your game and understand the emergent
possibilities created by the rules
■ Ascertain whether rules and gameplay elements are easily understood by players
■ Understand the emotional response that players have to your game
One critical thing that a paper prototype can't do is allow you—and playtesters—to see
how the game feels. This is the primary purpose of a digital prototype. Although you
could spend hours describing game mechanics to someone in detail, having them just
play the game and see how it feels is much more efficient (and more interesting). This is
discussed at length in the book Game Feel by Steve Swink.
1
In this chapter, you create a working game, and the end result will be something that
you can show to friends and colleagues. After letting them play it for a while, you can ask
whether the difficulty feels too easy, too difficult, or just right. Use that information to

SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Follow the standard project setup procedure outlined in Appendix A, "Standard
Project Setup Procedure," to create a new project in Unity. If you need a refresher
on the standard project setup procedure, see Appendix A.
■ Project Template: 3D Core
■ Project Name: Apple Picker
■ Scene Name: _Scene_0
■ Game Pane Dimensions: (you'll set these in the chapter)
You don't need to create any scripts at the beginning of this project, but you
should rename the default Sample Scene to _Scene_0 and follow the instructions
to set up the Game Pane, WebGL build, and Unity version control for this project.
It could save you a ton of time if anything goes wrong. Also make sure to choose
the IGDPD Layout for your Unity window.
Preparing
Happily, you already did a lot of the preparation for this prototype in Chapter 16,
"Thinking in Digital Systems," when we analyzed Apple Picker and the classic game
Kaboom!. As mentioned in that chapter, Apple Picker will have the same basic game
mechanics as Kaboom!. Understanding classic games and how they work is very useful
for you as a designer, and this is a nice easy game to start with.
Take a moment to look back at Chapter 16 and make sure that you understand the flow
charts for each element: the AppleTree, the Apple, and the Basket.
Getting Started: Art Assets
As a prototype, this game doesn't need fantastic art; it needs to work. The kind of art
that you'll create throughout much of this book is known as programmer art, which is
the placeholder art made by programmers that will eventually be replaced by the actual
game art created by artists. As with nearly everything in a prototype, the purpose of this
art is to get you from a concept to a working prototype as quickly as possible. If your
programmer art doesn't look terrible, that's nice, but it's certainly not necessary.

ORTHOGRAPHIC VERSUS PERSPECTIVE CAMERAS
Orthographic and perspective are two types of virtual 3D cameras, as shown in
Figure 29.8.
A perspective camera works like the human eye; because light comes in through
a lens, objects that are close to the camera appear large, and objects that are far
away appear smaller. This gives a perspective camera a field of view (a.k.a. projec-
tion) shaped like a square frustum (or more simply, a square pyramid with the top
cut off). You can see this in the top half of Figure 29.8. The pyramidal wireframe
shape extending out from the camera is the view frustum and shows everything
that the camera will see.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

Figure 29.8 Comparison of perspective and orthographic camera projections
Through an orthogonal camera, an object will appear to be the same size regard-
less of how far it is from the camera. The projection for an orthogonal camera is
rectangular rather than frustum shaped. This is shown in the bottom half of
Figure 29.8. The gray view frustum of an orthographic camera is a 3D rectangle
rather than a pyramid.

pane an orthographic camera looking straight down the Z axis. However, when

Game Panel Settings
Another contributing factor to your game view is the aspect ratio of the Game pane. The
aspect ratio is the relationship between the height and the width of the game view. The
orthographic Size that you just set in the Camera settings told Unity that there should
be 16m (i.e., 16 Unity units, which I sometimes abbreviate as meters) between the
center of the game view and the top and bottom edge of the view (for a total height of
32m). However, because of this, it's very important to be specific about the aspect ratio
of the Game pane as shown in Figure 29.9.
7
At the top of the Game pane is an aspect ratio pop-up menu that may currently display
Free Aspect. If so, this is something we need to fix:
1. Click the aspect ratio pop-up menu as shown in Figure 29.9.
2. Choose Full HD (1920x1080) from the menu.
1920x1080, or 1080p, is the standard "Full HD" resolution for high-definition television
and is the aspect ratio for many televisions and computer monitors. Unity's aspect ratio
menu also includes an option for 4K UHD (3840x2160) (or Ultra High Definition), which
is used by high-end modern console games, but for what we're doing—especially if you
the Scene pane is not locked in 2D mode, setting the Scene pane to be orthogonal
rather than perspective is also sometimes useful. To experiment with this:
■ Click the 2D button at the top of the Scene pane to exit 2D mode. This
will rotate into a 3D view of the scene.
■ Select the Main Camera so that you can see its rectangular frustum. This
will make the difference between the perspective and isometric scene
views clearer.
■ Click the word <Persp under the axes gizmo in the upper-right corner of
the Scene pane (shown in Figure 29.8). This will toggle the Scene pane
between perspective (abbreviated <Persp) and isometric (abbreviated =Iso)
scene views (isometric being another word for orthographic). Toggle
between the two a few times to see the difference.
■ Click the 2D button at the top of the Scene pane to return to 2D mode.
7. I have seen far too many projects look great inside the Unity editor on one computer and
absolutely awful on every other machine because the Game pane on the original computer
was set to Free Aspect. Don't do it!
